title: Accessibility in React: Focus and Interaction
summary: Build React interactions that work with semantic HTML, keyboards, focus, and assistive technology.

subtopics.title: Use semantic controls
subtopics.explanation: A semantic element communicates its purpose and often includes built-in keyboard behavior. Use a button for an action, a link for navigation, and a label for an input. A clickable `div` has none of those behaviors by default. Semantic HTML is like using a door handle instead of asking visitors to push a blank wall.

subtopics.title: Name controls clearly
subtopics.explanation: An accessible name tells assistive technology what a control does. Visible text inside a button usually supplies its name. Icon-only buttons need a label such as “Close dialog.” Inputs need connected labels. A placeholder disappears as people type, so it cannot replace a label. Clear names are like labels on switches in a control room.

subtopics.title: Manage focus in dialogs
subtopics.explanation: When a dialog opens, move focus into it and keep the keyboard path within its controls. When it closes, return focus to the button that opened it. Prefer the native `dialog` element when it fits. Focus is the keyboard’s pointer; moving it unexpectedly is like turning someone around without telling them.

subtopics.title: Announce changing status
subtopics.explanation: A screen reader may not notice text that appears elsewhere on the page. Use a polite live region for useful updates, such as “Three results loaded.” Do not announce every tiny change or move focus for routine status. Announcements should be like a quiet update from a guide, not an alarm for every step.

subtopics.title: Test the whole task
subtopics.explanation: Navigate with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and Escape where appropriate. Check visible focus, labels, heading order, and error recovery. Try at least one screen reader with the workflow. Automated scans can point to issues, but a person still needs to complete the task.

foundations.overview: Accessibility means people with different abilities can use the same interface. React does not make a custom control accessible automatically. Start with native buttons, labels, and headings. Then make focus movement predictable for dialogs and route changes, announce important asynchronous updates, and test the real user journey with a keyboard and screen reader.
foundations.mentalModel: A good interface is a public building with clear signs, reachable controls, and paths that work for different visitors.
foundations.whyItMatters: A visually clear interface can still fail when a keyboard cannot reach its controls or a screen reader cannot identify them.
foundations.formalDefinition: Frontend accessibility is the practice of making interface content and interactions perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust for people using varied abilities and assistive technologies.
foundations.browserPerspective: Browsers expose native roles, names, focus, and keyboard behavior through accessibility APIs that assistive tools can use.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use semantic elements first, then manage focus and status announcements only when the interaction needs them.
foundations.businessImpact: Accessible interfaces let more people complete tasks and reduce barriers across devices and input methods.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Accessible patterns belong in shared components so each page does not invent its own keyboard behavior.
foundations.performanceImpact: Accessible markup is usually lightweight; avoid adding complex custom widgets when native elements already work.
commonMisconceptions: ARIA alone makes a control accessible
ARIA adds information but does not supply missing keyboard behavior.
A visible focus ring is only decoration
It tells keyboard users which control will receive input.
Automated tools miss confusing labels and broken task flows.

keyTakeaways: A semantic element communicates its purpose and often includes built-in keyboard behavior.
An accessible name tells assistive technology what a control does.
When a dialog opens, move focus into it and keep the keyboard path within its controls.

codeLab.title: Return focus after a dialog closes
codeLab.instructions: Build a small dialog with an open button. Move focus into the dialog when it opens and return focus to the opener when it closes.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Keyboard users can open the dialog, reach its close button, and return to the opener.
hints: Break the task into state, event handling, and rendered feedback.
Keep the interface accessible with labels and meaningful button text.
